title: Spark ML: When to Use It, Pipelines, Estimators and Transformers

concepts.heading: When Spark ML Is the Right Tool
concepts.body: Databricks recommends training on a single machine when possible, because distributed code is more complex than single-machine code and slower from communication overhead. Consider distributed training when the data or the model is too large to fit in memory on one machine. Single-node libraries such as scikit-learn run in the Python process of the driver, so adding workers does not speed them up. Spark ML, the DataFrame-based pyspark.ml API, runs each algorithm as Spark jobs: rows stay in partitions on the workers and every pass combines partial results, so memory and compute grow with the cluster, and scoring can run where the data already lives. Choose Spark ML when the training set will not fit on one node, the algorithm exists in pyspark.ml and is accurate enough, and scoring also runs on Spark. Keep scikit-learn on one node when the table is small or the single-node model already wins: prepare features in Spark and read them with toPandas(). A flat learning curve also allows training on a representative sample. Parallelism follows partitions, so a table in 8 partitions keeps only 8 cores busy however large the cluster is.

concepts.heading: Estimators, Transformers and Pipelines
concepts.body: A Transformer implements transform(), which turns one DataFrame into another, usually by appending columns; feature transformers and fitted models are both Transformers. An Estimator implements fit(), which takes a DataFrame and produces a Model, and that Model is a Transformer. A Pipeline chains stages, each a Transformer or an Estimator, and runs them in order. A Pipeline is itself an Estimator: fit() returns a PipelineModel in which every Estimator has become a fitted Transformer. At scoring time the PipelineModel sends new data through the same learned processing, which is the main reason to put every step in the pipeline instead of preparing columns by hand. Because a Pipeline is an Estimator, one featurization Pipeline can be the first stage of several model pipelines, and a CrossValidator can tune the whole pipeline so preprocessing is refitted on each training fold. Stages must be unique instances, and a Pipeline checks types at run time against the DataFrame schema, not at compile time, so a missing or mistyped column fails only when the pipeline runs.

concepts.heading: Stages That Learn and Stages That Only Apply
concepts.body: Pick the stage by asking whether it must learn from training data. Estimators learn state that the fitted model keeps: StringIndexer maps strings to indices (frequencyDesc by default, so index 0 is the most frequent value) and IndexToString turns predictions back into labels; Imputer fills missing numeric values with the mean, median or mode; QuantileDiscretizer learns quantile splits and returns a Bucketizer, and may use fewer buckets than requested when there are few distinct values; StandardScaler and MaxAbsScaler learn column statistics. Row-level logic needs no learning: SQLTransformer runs a SELECT over __THIS__, so a derived column such as clicks / impressions becomes a saved pipeline stage. Two scaler details matter. StandardScaler has withMean false by default because centering builds a dense output, which is risky for sparse input, while MaxAbsScaler divides by the largest absolute value and keeps sparsity. KMeans uses distances, so scale features first or the widest range decides the clusters. Indices belong to the model that learned them: store raw categories in shared tables, not indexed values.

concepts.heading: Text, Vector and Streaming Stages
concepts.body: HashingTF is a Transformer that hashes terms into numFeatures buckets with MurmurHash 3. It needs no global dictionary, which suits a huge corpus, but different terms can collide and the mapping from position back to word is not kept. CountVectorizer is an Estimator that builds a vocabulary, limited by vocabSize and document-frequency thresholds such as minDF, and its model stores that vocabulary, so choose it when reviewers need the top words behind coefficients. VectorAssembler combines columns into one vector column and needs the size of every input vector. For a batch DataFrame Spark can inspect the data; in a streaming DataFrame the contents are not available until the stream starts, so place a VectorSizeHint(inputCol, size) stage before the assembler to put the size into the column metadata. Its handleInvalid option is error by default, with skip to drop bad rows and optimistic to skip the check. Missing values are another frequent failure: VectorAssembler rejects nulls by default, so impute inside the pipeline instead of dropping rows, which changes the population.

examPoints: Distributed training pays communication overhead: keep one node when the data and model fit in memory, and choose Spark ML when the training set will not fit and scoring also runs on Spark.

A Pipeline is an Estimator whose fit returns a PipelineModel; learned state (Imputer, StringIndexer, QuantileDiscretizer, scalers) lives in the fitted model, and stateless row logic belongs in SQLTransformer.
Match the stage to the symptom: MaxAbsScaler for sparse vectors, scaling before KMeans, CountVectorizer when words must be recovered, VectorSizeHint for vectors in a streaming DataFrame.

quiz.q: A media company keeps 1.2 billion click events in a Delta table. After feature encoding, the training set is larger than the memory of the biggest node type available. A logistic regression must be retrained nightly on the full history, and scoring runs later on the same Spark cluster. Which training approach fits?
choices: Move to a single-node cluster with the largest driver type and fit scikit-learn LogisticRegression after calling toPandas() on the whole training DataFrame
Keep scikit-learn on the driver and set n_jobs=-1, so that the worker cores of the cluster share the work of a single fit
Fit a Spark ML Pipeline that ends in LogisticRegression on the DataFrame, so the rows stay partitioned
Train scikit-learn on a 0.1% random sample, since the rare customer segments in the data add little to the model
quiz.explain: The training set does not fit in the memory of any single node, so a single-node fit is impossible. Spark ML keeps rows in partitions on the workers and combines partial results, and the same pipeline scores on Spark. A scikit-learn fit runs on the driver however many workers exist, so n_jobs cannot use them, and a tiny sample throws away the rare segments the business needs.

quiz.q: A 200-million-row churn table has nulls in income and tenure_months. The VectorAssembler stage fails on them, and filtering the null rows removes new customers. Scoring must reuse exactly the fill values learned on the training data. What should the team do?
choices: Add an Imputer with the median strategy before the VectorAssembler, so the fitted pipeline stores the medians
Replace the nulls with zero using DataFrame.fillna in the training notebook and repeat the same call in the scoring job
Set VectorAssembler handleInvalid to skip, so that rows containing nulls are removed at fit time and at scoring time
Compute the column medians with a separate aggregation job and write them as constants into the SQLTransformer statement
quiz.explain: Imputer is an Estimator: fit learns one surrogate value per column and the resulting model keeps it, so the PipelineModel applies the same numbers at scoring. Zero is a wrong fill for income and must be repeated by hand, skipping rows drops the new customers again, and hard-coded constants go stale and are not saved with the model.

recap: Use Spark ML when the data will not fit one node and scoring runs on Spark, otherwise stay on one machine. Put every learned step into a Pipeline so the PipelineModel repeats it at scoring, use SQLTransformer for stateless logic, and choose scalers and text stages by how they treat sparsity, vocabularies and streaming vector sizes.

title: Tuning, Evaluating and Scoring Spark ML Models

concepts.heading: Tuning with CrossValidator and TrainValidationSplit
concepts.body: MLlib tuning needs three things: an Estimator or a whole Pipeline, a list of ParamMaps and an Evaluator. CrossValidator splits the data into folds, averages the metric over the folds for each ParamMap, then refits the Estimator with the best ParamMap on the entire dataset. With 3 values of one parameter, 2 of another and 2 folds it trains (3 x 2) x 2 = 12 models. TrainValidationSplit evaluates each ParamMap once on a single train and validation pair set by trainRatio; it is cheaper but less reliable on small data. By default ParamMaps are evaluated in serial. Setting parallelism to 2 or more fits that many models at once; the docs say to choose it without exceeding cluster resources, that larger values may not help, and that up to 10 is generally enough. If each fit already fills the cluster, extra concurrency only competes for the same resources. foldCol names an integer column from 0 to numFolds minus 1 and replaces random folds, so a hash of customer_id keeps all rows of one customer in the same fold. Random folds leak groups and future rows.

concepts.heading: Choosing the Evaluator and Reading the Metric
concepts.body: The Evaluator decides which ParamMap wins, so match it to the task: RegressionEvaluator, BinaryClassificationEvaluator, MulticlassClassificationEvaluator, MultilabelClassificationEvaluator, RankingEvaluator, and ClusteringEvaluator for clustering. MulticlassClassificationEvaluator defaults to the f1 metric; for a rare class use a per-label metric such as recallByLabel together with metricLabel, whose default is 0. RankingEvaluator offers metrics such as ndcgAtK with k defaulting to 10, which judge a recommended list rather than a rating error. ClusteringEvaluator computes the silhouette from the features and prediction columns, so it needs no label and can pick k for KMeans. ALS returns NaN for users or items unseen in training, and an evaluator averaging NaN returns NaN; coldStartStrategy set to drop removes those rows so the metric is valid. A model summary describes the training set, so judge quality on a held-out split. The best average from CV is the maximum of many noisy estimates, so keep a test set that tuning never touches. A binary threshold defaults to 0.5; choose it on validation data against the business target.

concepts.heading: Batch and Streaming Scoring with a PipelineModel
concepts.body: A fitted PipelineModel scores with transform(), which is lazy and runs on the cluster. For a nightly batch, make the write idempotent: Delta mode overwrite with the replaceWhere option replaces only the rows that match a predicate, such as one score_date, so a retry cannot duplicate rows. Spark ML stores probabilities in a vector column that SQL users cannot index; vector_to_array turns it into an array of doubles. fit() needs a bounded dataset, so for streaming fit once on a static table, save the PipelineModel, and call transform on the streaming DataFrame. A stream-static join to a feature table is not stateful, so it needs no state management. For incremental scoring without a cluster running all day, schedule a job with trigger(availableNow=True): it processes what is available when it starts, then stops, and a checkpoint remembers progress. A model loaded once at start-up is not refreshed when an alias later moves, so restart the query or load the model per micro-batch.

concepts.heading: Spark ML or a Single-Node Model for Inference
concepts.body: Inference style decides the design, not the training tool. Batch over very large tables wants throughput: a Spark ML PipelineModel runs transform in the JVM next to the data, and a single-node model can still be scaled out with mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf, which applies the model to partitions on the workers. A few thousand rows fit one small node: load the model with mlflow.pyfunc.load_model and call predict on pandas, because starting executors costs more than the scoring. For deep models stored as files, pyspark.ml.functions.predict_batch_udf takes a make_predict_fn that loads the model and caches its predict function, so the load is not repeated for every batch. Streaming should score inside the query, with spark_udf or an iterator pandas UDF, not by collecting each micro-batch with toPandas() to the driver, where batch size is unbounded. Real-time requests of one row cannot pay Spark job start-up: register the model and create a Model Serving endpoint. With equal accuracy, a Spark ML pipeline needs no Python workers or matching Python packages.

examPoints: CrossValidator averages the metric over folds and refits the best ParamMap on all data; TrainValidationSplit evaluates once; parallelism helps only when fits do not already fill the cluster, and foldCol keeps groups together.

Match the evaluator to the task (recallByLabel with metricLabel for a rare class, RankingEvaluator for recommendation lists, ClusteringEvaluator for unlabeled KMeans) and report quality on a test set that tuning never saw.

Fit on static data and call transform on a stream; use replaceWhere for idempotent batch writes, availableNow for incremental scheduled scoring, spark_udf for batch scale-out and Model Serving for one-row real-time calls.

quiz.q: A fraud model is tuned with CrossValidator(numFolds=5). Each customer has many transactions, and cross-validation scores are far higher than the scores seen on new customers after deployment. Which change addresses the cause?
choices: Raise numFolds from 5 to 10 so that every fold holds fewer transactions from any customer
Add a fold column such as abs(hash(customer_id)) % 5 and pass it with setFoldCol
Replace CrossValidator by TrainValidationSplit with trainRatio 0.8, which evaluates each ParamMap once
Set parallelism to 10 so that the folds run at the same time and the random split is repeated several times
quiz.explain: Random folds spread one customer's rows across training and validation, so the model is scored on customers it has already seen. foldCol takes an integer from 0 to numFolds minus 1 and replaces the random split, so hashing the customer key keeps each customer in a single fold. More folds and a random single split still mix customers, and parallelism changes speed, not the split.

quiz.q: A streaming job reads events with spark.readStream and tries to run Pipeline([StringIndexer(...), VectorAssembler(...), LogisticRegression()]).fit on the streaming DataFrame. Spark rejects it. What is the correct design?
choices: Call fit inside foreachBatch on every micro-batch, so that the pipeline is refitted continuously on the newest events
Add a watermark to the streaming DataFrame before calling fit, so that the pipeline sees a bounded window of events
Convert the stream to pandas with toPandas() and fit a scikit-learn pipeline once for each micro-batch of events
Fit on a static training table once, save the PipelineModel, and call its transform on the streaming DataFrame
quiz.explain: fit makes several passes over the data and needs a bounded dataset, while a streaming DataFrame can only run through writeStream. A fitted PipelineModel only applies learned state, so transform works on a stream. Refitting per micro-batch changes the learned mapping and the model with every batch, a watermark does not make a stream finite, and toPandas() on a stream is not available.

recap: Tune whole pipelines with CrossValidator, use foldCol or a time split to stop leakage, and report the metric on an untouched test set. Match the evaluator to the task, fit pipelines on static data and transform on streams, and pick the inference path by volume and latency: Spark ML or spark_udf for batch, one small node for small tables, Model Serving for single rows.

title: Scaling Training with Spark ML and pandas Function APIs

concepts.heading: Keeping Spark ML Training Busy
concepts.body: Spark ML algorithms are ordinary Spark jobs, so one task processes one partition. If the training DataFrame has 8 partitions, at most 8 cores work on each pass, so compare the tasks in the Spark UI stage with the total executor cores and repartition to a small multiple of the core count, for example 320 for 10 workers with 16 cores. Iterative solvers such as logistic regression read the data once per iteration, and Spark evaluates DataFrames lazily. Without persistence, every pass re-runs the whole lineage of reads, joins and feature stages, so cache the assembled training DataFrame and run an action to materialize it before calling fit. When many small models train from the same features, fit them concurrently: the Spark job scheduling guide says that multiple parallel jobs can run inside one application if they are submitted from separate threads, and a fit is a set of jobs. Cache the shared features first. Prefer built-in column functions such as log1p and arithmetic on columns over Python UDFs, because they run in the JVM with no Python worker or serialization.

concepts.heading: pandas Function APIs and Their Limits
concepts.body: pandas function APIs apply a native Python function to pandas objects and use Apache Arrow to move data. There are three kinds. Grouped map, groupBy().applyInPandas(), is split-apply-combine: the function receives all rows of one group as a pandas DataFrame and returns a pandas DataFrame, and you supply a schema as a StructType or a string. Map, mapInPandas(), receives an iterator of pandas DataFrames and returns an iterator, so output can have any length. Cogrouped map, groupBy().cogroup().applyInPandas(), shuffles two DataFrames so groups with the same key meet, and the function receives two pandas DataFrames, which suits train and holdout pairs per key and as-of joins. Returned column labels must match the schema field names (or match by position when not named by strings). All data of a group or cogroup is loaded into memory first, so skewed groups can run out of memory, and maxRecordsPerBatch does not apply to groups. For plain pandas UDFs, Spark converts partitions to Arrow record batches, and lowering spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch (default 10,000) reduces memory use on wide rows.

concepts.heading: One Model per Group
concepts.body: Training a model per store, region or customer fits grouped map well: groupBy(key).applyInPandas(train_fn, schema) runs one call per group, groups run in parallel across the cluster, and each group can use any single-node library. Return something the schema can carry: the key, a metric and, in a binary column, the pickled model bytes, so a Delta table can hold both results and models. Parallelism equals the number of groups. With 12 regions only 12 tasks work, however large the cluster is. To tune per region, cross join the regions with a small table of candidate configurations and group by region and config id, so each pair is an independent task. Group size is bounded by one node, so very large groups need Spark ML instead. For inference per group or at scale, mapInPandas lets you load the model once before iterating over batches and yield a result for each batch, whereas a Series-to-Series pandas UDF repeats the load in its body for each batch. Return metrics to the driver and log them to MLflow from there.

examPoints: Spark ML parallelism follows partitions: repartition to a multiple of the cores, cache the training DataFrame for iterative solvers, and submit independent fits from separate threads.
applyInPandas gives one call per group with the whole group in memory; cogroup passes two DataFrames per key; mapInPandas passes an iterator of batches and returns any number of rows.
Per-group parallelism is capped by the number of groups and a group must fit one node; load models once before the loop in mapInPandas and return model bytes in a binary column.

quiz.q: A tuning job fits one model per region for 12 regions using groupBy('region').applyInPandas(fit_and_score, schema) on a cluster with 400 cores. Each candidate configuration is evaluated one after another inside the function, and most cores stay idle. Which redesign uses the cluster?
choices: Raise spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to 400 so that the 12 regions are spread over all the available cores
Lower spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch so that each region is split into smaller Arrow batches
Replace applyInPandas with a Series-to-Series pandas UDF that receives the regions as separate columns
Cross join regions with the configurations and group by region and config id
quiz.explain: applyInPandas makes one call per group and sends all rows of a group to one task, so 12 groups keep at most 12 tasks busy whatever the shuffle partition count is. Making each region and configuration pair its own group creates many independent tasks. maxRecordsPerBatch does not apply to groups, and a pandas UDF over columns does not train per region.

quiz.q: A 1.5 GB scikit-learn model scores an 800-million-row table with a Series-to-Series pandas UDF that calls joblib.load in its body. Executors spend most of their time reading the model file. What change removes that cost?
choices: Use groupBy().applyInPandas() with the customer key, so that each group loads the model once
Use mapInPandas, load the model once before iterating over the batches and yield a result for each batch
Raise spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch above the default, so that fewer batches call the function
Call toPandas() on the table and score it in a single loop on the driver where the model is loaded once
quiz.explain: The body of a Series-to-Series pandas UDF runs for every Arrow batch, so the model is loaded again each time. mapInPandas passes an iterator, and code before the loop runs once per task. Grouped map loads the file for every group, a bigger batch size risks memory errors on wide rows, and toPandas() collects 800 million rows on the driver.

recap: Make Spark ML use the whole cluster with enough partitions, cached training data and concurrent fits from separate threads. Use applyInPandas for one model per group, cogroup for paired data and mapInPandas for efficient inference, remembering that parallelism equals the number of groups and that a group must fit in memory.

title: Distributed Hyperparameter Tuning with Optuna and Ray

concepts.heading: Optuna Studies, Samplers and Pruners
concepts.body: Optuna is an open-source library for hyperparameter tuning that can scale horizontally. The search space is declared inside the objective function with trial.suggest_* calls, and the objective returns the value to optimize, for example a validation error. A range that spans many orders of magnitude needs log=True, as in trial.suggest_float('svr_c', 1e-10, 1e10, log=True), otherwise almost all samples land in the top decade. A Study is the record of finished trials. A sampler reads that record to choose the next parameters, and a pruner stops trials that look worse than earlier trials at the same step. The Databricks MlflowSparkStudy uses TPESampler as the default sampler and MedianPruner as the default pruner. Pruning needs intermediate values, so the objective must report a value to the trial after each epoch or fold and stop when the trial is marked for pruning; a pruner cannot judge a trial that reports only at the end. Hyperopt with SparkTrials is a legacy path no longer maintained; its hp expressions outside the objective become suggest calls inside it.

concepts.heading: Distributing Optuna with MlflowSparkStudy
concepts.body: Databricks documents two classes added with MLflow 3.0. MlflowStorage lets Optuna use the MLflow tracking server, one experiment, as its storage backend, and it batches writes to avoid REST API throttling. MlflowSparkStudy wraps an Optuna Study to run parallel trials on PySpark executors. The pattern is: create MlflowStorage(experiment_id=...), create MlflowSparkStudy(study_name=..., storage=...), then call optimize(objective, n_trials=..., n_jobs=...) and read best_params. The storage must be shared, because with the default in-memory storage every worker keeps its own record, so 40 workers run 40 separate searches that never learn from each other. MLflow 3.0 is preinstalled in Databricks Runtime 17.1 ML and above; on older runtimes run %pip install mlflow --upgrade and %pip install optuna at the top of the notebook. If the import of MlflowSparkStudy fails, a runtime without MLflow 3 is the first thing to check. Each trial is tracked in the experiment, which gives a comparable history of parameters and values. The trial function must be a single-node training function, because each trial runs inside one Spark task.

concepts.heading: Ray Tune on Databricks
concepts.body: Ray is an open-source framework for scaling Python applications, and Ray Tune provides scalable hyperparameter search. On Databricks, ray.util.spark.setup_ray_cluster starts a background Spark job in which each Spark task becomes a Ray worker node, and the Ray head node runs on the driver. Ray on Spark is supported on dedicated access mode, no isolation shared access mode and jobs clusters only; it cannot start on serverless compute. A cluster made in a notebook belongs to that user and shuts down when the notebook detaches or after 30 minutes without tasks. setup_global_ray_cluster, Ray 2.9.0 and above, makes a global mode cluster that every user on the compute can reach with ray.init(), with no inactivity timeout. Avoid %pip on a running Ray cluster because it shuts it down; install libraries first. For MLflow with Ray 2.41 and above, set DATABRICKS_HOST and a token, or a client ID and secret, as environment variables before setup_ray_cluster. Log from the driver, or give each task the parent run ID and start a child run. For hybrid GPU jobs set spark.task.resource.gpu.amount to 0, so Spark preprocessing leaves the GPUs to Ray.

concepts.heading: Choosing Between Optuna on Spark and Ray
concepts.body: Both tools run many independent trials. Use Optuna with MlflowSparkStudy when each trial is a single-node function, such as a scikit-learn or boosted-tree fit, you already run on a standard Databricks cluster, and you want the study and every trial recorded in one MLflow experiment with sampler and pruner choices. Use Ray Tune when trials are dynamic or GPU-heavy, when trials run for very different times and new work depends on earlier results, when analysts must share one long-lived cluster, or when the code already uses Ray Train. The budget is shared: with a fixed number of GPUs, trial-level parallelism has almost no communication cost, whereas data parallelism inside a trial synchronizes at every step, so several trials on a few devices each often beat every trial on all devices in sequence. Neither tool replaces the choice of search algorithm: TPE and similar samplers learn from results, random search does not. Keep Hyperopt out of new designs because it is not maintained and is not in ML Runtime after 16.4 LTS.

examPoints: Distributed Optuna on Databricks needs shared storage: MlflowStorage on one experiment plus MlflowSparkStudy, which defaults to TPESampler and MedianPruner; MLflow 3.0 is preinstalled from Runtime 17.1 ML, otherwise install it with %pip.
Search spaces live inside the objective (suggest_float with log=True for wide ranges) and pruning works only if the objective reports intermediate values.

Ray on Spark needs dedicated, no isolation shared or jobs compute (not serverless), setup_global_ray_cluster shares one cluster, %pip stops a running cluster, and MLflow credentials must be set before setup_ray_cluster.

quiz.q: A team starts 40 parallel Optuna workers on Spark. Each worker builds its own study with the default in-memory storage, and the best value barely improves compared with 4 workers. How should the team fix the setup?
choices: Create the study on MlflowStorage and run it through MlflowSparkStudy, so all workers share one record
Give every worker a different random seed and merge the 40 best_params dictionaries by hand after the runs finish
Increase n_trials on each worker and keep the in-memory storage, so each worker explores a larger share of the space
Switch the sampler to RandomSampler on every worker, since a sampler that learns from trials needs more memory per trial
quiz.explain: With in-memory storage each worker keeps its own list of trials, so 40 independent searches run and no sampler sees the others' results. MlflowStorage uses the MLflow tracking server as shared storage, and MlflowSparkStudy runs the parallel trials on executors against it. Seeds, more trials and a random sampler leave the searches independent.

quiz.q: A data scientist runs a long Ray Tune search and then runs %pip install lightgbm in the same notebook. The search stops and the Ray cluster disappears. What is the documented practice?
choices: Use setup_global_ray_cluster, because a global mode cluster is not affected by library installation in a notebook
Attach the notebook to serverless compute, which keeps the Ray cluster alive while the Python environment restarts
Install the libraries before the Ray cluster is created, at the top of the notebook or as cluster libraries
Set DATABRICKS_HOST and a token as environment variables so that Ray reconnects after the package installation
quiz.explain: The Ray cluster is started from the notebook as a background Spark job, and running %pip on a running Ray cluster shuts it down. Libraries should be installed first, then setup_ray_cluster and ray.init. Serverless compute cannot host Ray on Spark, and credentials only matter for MLflow calls from tasks.

recap: Declare the Optuna search space in the objective, report intermediate values for pruning, and share one study across workers with MlflowStorage and MlflowSparkStudy. Choose Ray Tune for dynamic or GPU-heavy trials on a supported cluster, install libraries before creating the Ray cluster, and set MLflow credentials before setup_ray_cluster.

title: Scaling Strategy: Vertical vs Horizontal, Data vs Model Parallelism, Ray vs Spark

concepts.heading: Vertical or Horizontal Scaling
concepts.body: Vertical scaling means a bigger machine with more memory, cores or GPUs; horizontal scaling means more machines. Databricks advises training neural networks on a single machine when possible, because distributed training and inference code is more complex and slower due to communication overhead, and says to consider distribution when the model or the data cannot fit in memory on one machine. So scale up first: the code stays the same, debugging is easy, and a multi-GPU node avoids the network. Vertical scaling stops at the largest instance, and that node is a single point of failure, so plan to scale out when data keeps growing. Horizontal scaling adds memory and compute but pays synchronization costs, so returns diminish: a job on 8 nodes may speed up much less than 8 times because every step ends with an exchange between processes. Use the fewest machines that meet the time target. For classical algorithms, Databricks offers distributed Spark ML training through pyspark.ml.connect; from Databricks Runtime 17.0 Spark ML is enabled by default in Standard compute.

concepts.heading: Data Parallelism and Model Parallelism
concepts.body: Data parallelism keeps a full copy of the model in every process, divides the data into shards, and averages gradients between processes. Choose it when the model fits one device but the dataset or the number of steps is large. TorchDistributor launches PyTorch training as Spark jobs through torch.distributed.run; its arguments are num_processes, local_mode and use_gpu. Put imports such as import torch inside the training function to avoid pickling errors. With DistributedDataParallel, each process builds its own DataLoader, so pass a DistributedSampler or every process reads the full dataset. Use the nccl backend on GPUs and gloo on CPUs. The error ncclInternalError: Internal check failed means NCCL cannot use some network interfaces; the documented fix is os.environ['NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME'] = 'eth0' in the training code. Model parallelism splits the model across devices because one copy does not fit; adding more replicas then only adds failures. The DeepSpeed distributor, built on TorchDistributor, is the recommended solution for models that need more compute but are limited by memory, with optimized memory use and pipeline parallelism.

concepts.heading: Ray and Spark Side by Side
concepts.body: Databricks describes Ray and Spark as complementary. Spark specializes in data parallelism: one operation over partitions of a large dataset, as in ETL, joins, aggregations and Spark ML. Ray excels at logical parallelism: many dynamic, compute-intensive tasks such as tuning, deep learning, reinforcement learning and per-item time series forecasting. Spark runs a fixed plan of stages, so a second pass whose size depends on first results needs another job, while Ray tasks can be launched as results arrive. Ray on Databricks keeps the platform benefits: Unity Catalog governance, MLflow tracking, Lakeflow Jobs, and Model Serving for models trained with Ray Train, so training with Ray does not mean leaving Databricks. A typical pipeline aggregates terabytes with Spark and then trains or tunes with Ray on the same cluster. Size the Ray cluster deliberately: setting num_cpus_worker_node to the CPU cores and num_gpus_worker_node to the GPUs of each Spark worker makes each worker launch one Ray worker using all its resources. The Ray head defaults to 0 CPUs and 0 GPUs. With a fixed node count, enable autoscaling so idle Ray workers free the nodes for Spark.

concepts.heading: A Decision Guide for Large-Scale Training
concepts.body: Work through the choice in order. First, does it fit one node? If yes, train there, using a larger or multi-GPU instance if needed, and keep Spark for feature preparation. Second, what is the algorithm? A classical algorithm that exists in pyspark.ml, such as logistic regression on a 2 TB Delta table, belongs in Spark ML, which is already a data-parallel job over a DataFrame. Third, for a deep-learning model that fits on one GPU but trains on huge data, use data parallelism with TorchDistributor or Ray Train. Fourth, if the weights and optimizer state do not fit one GPU, use DeepSpeed or another model-parallel approach. Fifth, for thousands of independent, uneven, stateful or dynamically created tasks, use Ray. Finally, split a fixed GPU budget: running several trials, each on a few devices, usually beats running each trial across all devices one after another, because independent trials need no communication. A single-node library does not distribute by itself: n_jobs uses the driver cores only.

examPoints: Start with one machine and scale up; distribute only when data or model exceed memory, and expect diminishing returns from synchronization when adding nodes.
Data parallelism copies the model per process (TorchDistributor with a DistributedSampler); when one copy does not fit, use the DeepSpeed distributor; NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME fixes ncclInternalError.
Spark is data parallelism for ETL and Spark ML, Ray is logical parallelism for dynamic compute tasks; set num_cpus_worker_node and num_gpus_worker_node to the per-worker hardware.

quiz.q: A vision team has a model that fits comfortably in the memory of one GPU, but its 4 TB image dataset takes days to train on one machine. Which approach is the best fit?
choices: Pipeline parallelism with the DeepSpeed distributor, because the model must be split across several GPUs
A larger driver for a single scikit-learn fit, since distributed training is always slower than one machine
Data parallelism with TorchDistributor, so each process holds the full model and reads its own data shard
Spark ML LogisticRegression on the image bytes, so that the table is processed in parallel across workers
quiz.explain: Because the model fits one device, replicas are possible and data parallelism divides the dataset among processes, which averages gradients to keep copies identical. Splitting the model, as DeepSpeed does, is for weights that do not fit. A single-machine fit does not finish in time for this much data, and Spark ML does not replace a vision network.

quiz.q: A cluster has 6 worker nodes, each with 48 cores and 4 GPUs. The team wants every Spark worker to host exactly one Ray worker that can use all of its cores and GPUs for Ray Tune. Which setup call does this?
choices: setup_ray_cluster(max_worker_nodes=24), so that each of the 4 GPUs of a node gets a separate Ray worker
setup_ray_cluster(max_worker_nodes=6, num_cpus_worker_node=48, num_gpus_worker_node=4)
setup_ray_cluster(max_worker_nodes=6, num_cpus_head_node=48, num_gpus_head_node=4), giving the head the hardware
setup_global_ray_cluster(max_worker_nodes=1), because a global cluster claims every GPU of the compute for itself
quiz.explain: The Databricks guidance is to set num_cpus_worker_node to the cores and num_gpus_worker_node to the GPUs of each Spark worker, so each worker launches one Ray worker that uses all of its resources. The head node mostly coordinates and defaults to no CPUs or GPUs, 24 workers would not match the hardware, and a global cluster concerns sharing, not sizing.

recap: Scale up before out, and distribute only when data or model exceed one machine. Use data parallelism when the model fits a device, DeepSpeed when it does not, Spark ML for classical algorithms on big tables, Ray for dynamic compute-heavy tasks, and size Ray workers to the hardware of each Spark worker.
